story.text: Once upon a time in the 1960s, a boy and a girl met at college. We’ll call them Robert and Linda.
A few years later, during an unusually rainy season in January, they started dating.
Then a few years after that, they got married.
Eventually they had two kids, bought a single-family home, and built successful careers.

Decades later, in 2017, Robert was asked how his relationship is.


He said it was excellent.

Robert is one of the thousands of people Stanford University researchers have been [tracking](https://data.stanford.edu/hcmst2017) to understand how couples meet, how they separate, and what their relationships is like. But it’s 2017, so a global pandemic is coming soon. Relationships will be strained. Single people will have to reinvent dating. It will be a profound test of what we expect of partnerships in the modern day.
This piece only visualizes people who participated in every wave of this survey.
For now, most partnered people say their relationships are quite good.

Men are slightly more likely to say their relationship is excellent.


>> Chart Data|filler
People with more money tend to report better relationships—partially because they have more time and resources to devote to their partners.
The other factor is that older people tend to have more money, and they’ve had more time to find and develop high-quality relationships.
But over time, fewer and fewer people have said their relationships are excellent.

Over the last few decades, we’ve seen some concerning trends in American relationships. 


More people report being unsatisfied with their marriage.


>> Marriage satisfaction Data|filler


And the dynamics in those relationships have shifted in worrying ways.


Researchers studied how relationships have changed from 1987 to 2013. They found that in both [marriages](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36683860/) and [cohabitating partnerships](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11113-025-09982-y), couples report lower levels of fairness and higher levels of disagreement. Most concerning is that they also reported lower levels of interaction, [possibly](https://www.theatlantic.com/health/archive/2017/09/we-expect-way-too-much-from-our-romantic-partners/541353/) because many Americans are working longer hours which leaves less time for their partnership. 


>> Charts Data|filler


Given these circumstances, some researchers suspected that a societal disruption could expose the fractures in our relationships—eroding the quality of our partnerships, and even breaking them. This is called [stress theory](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7644604/), which argues that these stressors actually use up the very energy we need to support our partners through it. This is especially true of more [chronic stressors](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S2352250X16300690), like financial strain and long-term illness, which constantly sip away at the emotional capacity we need to care for both a relationship and our own well-being.


But if couples can successfully navigate these challenges, researchers have found that it brings couples closer together—a framework called [resilience theory](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1545-5300.2003.00001.x). They are able to build a shared meaning of the threat, come up with a plan, and rely on each other to weather the events.

It’s 2020. A global pandemic begins.


Within the confines of their locked down home, Robert and Linda have agreed that they should socially distance and wear masks in public.
They haven’t fought much during lockdown, unlike some couples.

In fact, Robert says his relationship is still excellent—just like before.


Not a huge surprise, given that they’ve been together for more than 50 years!
But what happened to everyone else we met in 2017?

story.text: From 2017 to several months into the pandemic, most married people stayed together. Unmarried partners were far more likely to break up. And sadly several people’s partners died.

story.text: But even among people who stayed together, many said they fought with their partner multiple times in the past week.
If we look at how people assessed their relationships in 2017…

story.text: … we can see that by fall 2020, a lot of people rated their relationship worse than it was before.

story.chart_title: How relationship quality changes from 2017 to 2020
story.text:
Love stories hypnotize us with scripts of what a relationship should look like. They give us templates for courting, proposals, marriage, and even domestic life.


Those stories shape the expectations we have of our relationships—but those expectations have shifted drastically over time. [Historians](https://www.jstor.org/stable/3600162) often break down modern conceptions of American marriage into three eras. 


>> Three eras|filler


**Before the 1850s**, marriage was about survival. Partnerships were about ensuring financial success, while continuing your family line. It certainly wasn’t about a strong emotional connection with another person.


**From the 1850s to 1960s**, marriage slowly became more about companionship—but following a rigid script. People were expected to fill specific gender roles as breadwinners, homemakers, and parents. Furthermore, sex and children were only socially acceptable in a marriage, so almost everyone got married.


>> Charts on marriage rates + median age of marriage|filler


But during this era, something was brewing under the surface. Sociologist Francesca Cancian analyzed the kind of marriage advice popular magazines offered during this period, and found that these rigid and traditional expectations eroded and were replaced by expectations that allowed individuals to shape their marriage based on their own preferences.


In other words, people rebelled against the stories.

>> Cancian Data|filler


**Since the 1960s**, marriage became less about fulfilling societal gender roles, and more about negotiating a partnership that works for us both inside and outside our relationships. In other words, we want a partner who can allow us to develop into the person we want to be. 


Sociologist Eli J. Finkel [argues](https://www.nytimes.com/2014/02/15/opinion/sunday/the-all-or-nothing-marriage.html) that our evolving expectations of marriage have followed Maslow’s hierarchy of needs. Initially we chose our relationships based on survival; then we wanted to feel loved; and then we wanted relationships that helped us be the people we want to be.


>> Maslow Psychological well being/safety, belonging/love, self-actualization|filler


That said, the classic love story still captures our imaginations. So that means we want relationships that provide security, passion, intellectual stimulation, and personal growth. We expect more from our partners than ever before—an “all-or-nothing” arrangement, Finkel [says](https://www.amazon.com/All-Nothing-Marriage-Best-Marriages/dp/052595516X).


When our relationships can’t meet our high and sometimes rigid expectations, we’re unsatisfied.


But when our relationships live up to these expectations—especially in the face of an external threat—we’re happier than ever.
Here is how people rated the quality of their relationships in 2020. When asked how the pandemic changed their relationship…

story.chart_title: How the pandemic changed their relationship, 2020
story.text:
… a large chunk of people who were in excellent relationships said it actually improved their relationship even more! 


In other words, their relationships were already excellent—but they said it grew even stronger.

story.chart_title: How the pandemic changed their relationship, 2020
story.text: Meanwhile, the pandemic was far more likely to erode the quality of less-than-excellent relationships.

story.chart_title: How the pandemic changed their relationship, 2022
story.text:
And two years later, even more people in excellent relationships said that the pandemic improved their partnership.


>> Chart|filler

story.chart_title: How the pandemic changed their relationship, 2022
story.text:
Stanford researchers [found](https://web.stanford.edu/~mrosenfe/Rosenfeld_Hausen_Resilience_Stress_Soc_Sci_2023.pdf) that the pandemic allowed couples to spend more time together—something many of them lacked because of commuting and work. Furthermore, they found that functional couples engaged in “mutual meaning making.” They aligned their perspectives on the virus’s risk, and agreed on how they would behave in response to it.


>> Chart|filler
Still, people often focus on the fact that fewer people report having excellent relationships.

And they point out that there are more single people now than ever before.


>> Chart Data|filler

Furthermore, young people are [less interested](https://www.rasmussenreports.com/public_content/lifestyle/general_lifestyle/june_2025/dating_37_of_young_singles_aren_t_interested) in pursuing relationships.


>> Find chart|filler

The lack of interest in a love life might be because the courting process is mostly happening online—and people [really don’t enjoy](https://www.theatlantic.com/technology/archive/2024/04/dating-apps-are-starting-crack/678022/) that experience.


>> Chart Data|filler
Taken together, it seems young people are embracing elements of the traditional love story, along with the associated gender roles.

A [recent survey](https://www.kcl.ac.uk/news/almost-a-third-of-gen-z-men-agree-a-wife-should-obey-her-husband) found that Gen Z men worldwide are more likely to have traditional views on relationships than the last three generations. Compared to older generations, more of them believe that wives should always obey their husbands; that women should not be too independent; and that we’ve gone too far in supporting women’s equality and we’re now discriminating against men.


About [90%](https://phys.org/news/2022-02-discrepancy-hookup-culture-sexual-dates.html) of dates among young people are initiated by men, even though almost everyone agrees that it’s OK for a woman to ask out a man.


And women in heterosexual relationships still do [more household work](https://fraser.stlouisfed.org/files/docs/releases/atus/atus_20250626.pdf) than men. And this doesn’t even include the [mental labor](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0003122419859007) women do to keep a household functioning.


The traditional love story, and its associated gender roles, are enduring. 


But so many of us know it’s not working for us. This story produces a world that expects women to be submissive and deferential to men, while doing most of the domestic work. It expects men to play the role of provider and protector, even when their families need them to be nurturers and caretakers. It expects us to play the roles of boy and girl, man and woman, husband and wife—even when none of these roles fit who we are.

That’s why many successful couples rewrite the script. They work together to figure out a story that works for them. 


It’s hard work—certainly less glamorous compared to the impulsive, exciting, and hopeful feelings of an early relationship.
But if we want to love our partners as full people, and not just actors in our imaginary stories, we have to let go of the fairy tales and do the work of writing our own stories.
